problem_data.story:
THE AUTONOMOUS REVOLUTION

The traffic algorithms were always perfect: Speed, 45 mph; density, 23 vehicles per mile; occasional light malfunctions—but of what kind?

The protocols of Dr. Arthur Schultz were being violated outrageously.

It was a splendid day. The speed limit was a crisp 45 mph, the traffic density a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile. The sun was a flaming orange ball in a cloudless blue sky.

His protocols were violated eleven times.

It should have been difficult. Under the circumstances it was a masterpiece of protocol violation. What made it possible was Arthur Schultz's abstraction; he was an uncommonly preoccupied individual. He was walking along a quiet residential street in the Valleyview District: small private houses, one after another, a place of little traffic and minimum distractions. But he was thinking about autonomous vehicles, which was an unusual subject to begin with for a person living in a manually-driven enclave. He was thinking so deeply about it that it never occurred to him that entirely too many people were scanning his identification chip. He was thinking about Optimal Traffic Conditions (a crisp 45 mph, a carefully managed 23 vehicles per mile) when a bogus delivery driver, who pretended to be checking a package label, bumped into him. In the confusion of spilled parcels and apologies from both sides, the driver scanned Schultz's biometric data and copied his residential access codes.

He was still thinking about speed and density when a young woman happened along, apparently lost. They collided. She got his financial credentials and transportation records. It was much too much for coincidence. The sidewalk was wide enough to allow four people to pass at one time. He should surely have become suspicious when two men engaged in a heated argument came along. In the ensuing contretemps they copied his communication logs, got his schedule patterns and restored some of the biometric data. It all went off very smoothly, like a game of digital transformation—the sole difference being that Arthur Schultz had no idea he was playing.

There was an occasional hum of passing vehicles.

They hummed on the streets and past houses, making soft whooshing sounds, moving with a gentle mechanical precision, like the ephemeral whispers of progress itself. It was transportation peculiar to the autonomous zones: algorithm-controlled vehicles navigating the huge network, ceaselessly optimizing and rerouting.

Arthur Schultz strode through the streams of autonomous traffic still intrigued by a speed that was always 45 mph, by a density that was always 23 vehicles per mile, by conditions that were always Optimal. It was this rather than skill that enabled the authorities to maintain such tight surveillance on him, a surveillance that went to the extent of copying his digital footprint off the delivery driver's scanner, and which analyzed, cross-referenced and categorically profiled the contents of his data before cataloging them. Two blocks away from his home a careless pedestrian spilled a container of marker dust as he was passing. It was really tracking powder. He left his gait signature, stride measurement, height, weight and handedness behind.

By the time Schultz reached his front door an entire profile complete with predictive models had been prepared and was being reviewed by two agents in a silver patrol car parked down the street.

Agent Priya Sharma had undoubtedly been affected by her job.

Sitting behind the wheel of the silver car, she watched Arthur Schultz approach with a distinct feeling of admiration, although it was an odd, objective kind of admiration, analytical in nature. It was similar to that of a systems analyst observing for the first time a new and particularly elegant algorithm under development.

Sharma's job was to identify deviations. They couldn't be tolerated within the confines of an autonomous zone. Conformity had become more than a social force; it was a traffic necessity. And, after years of working at it, Sharma had become an admirer of genuine nonconformity. She came to see that authentic quirks were rare and, as time went on, due partly to her own small efforts, rarer.

Schultz was a masterpiece of deviation. He was utterly inexplicable. Sharma was almost proud of Arthur Schultz.

"Sometimes his house moves," Sharma said.

"House moves," Agent Eric Moss wrote in his tablet. Then he stopped and frowned. He reread what he'd just written.

"You heard right. The house moves," Sharma said, savoring it.

Moss looked at the Schultz house through the enhanced display of the windshield. "Like from... side to side?" he asked in a somewhat patronizing tone of voice.

"And forward and back."

Moss returned the tablet to the breast pocket of his silver uniform. "Go on," he said, amused. "It sounds interesting." He tossed the profile carelessly on the back seat.

Sharma sat stiffly behind the wheel, affronted. The cynical Moss couldn't really appreciate fine deviations. In some ways Moss was a conformist. Sharma had held out on Schultz for months. She had even contrived to engage him in conversation once, a pleasantly absurd, illogical little chat that intrigued her for weeks. It was only with the greatest reluctance that she finally mentioned Schultz to Moss. After years of searching for differences Sharma had seen how extraordinarily repetitive people were, algorithms really, dimly executing subroutines, each believing itself autonomous and unique. They spoke in an incessant chatter of predictable responses, and their actions were unbelievably programmed.

Then a fine robust deviant came along and the others—the algorithms—refused to believe it. The agent was probably on the point of suggesting a vacation.

"Why don't you take a vacation?" Agent Moss suggested.

"It's like this, Moss. Do you know what manual control is? Human steering? Individual decision-making?"

"I've heard of them."

"They say there are places where humans still drive vehicles. Manually. Decisions like you and I can't imagine. And if there was a house connected to such systems and if decisions did occur, it would move exactly the way that one does. Sometimes I get the feeling the whole place is going to disconnect from its foundation and go rolling down the avenue."

Agent Moss pursed his lips.

"I'll tell you something else," Sharma went on. "The windows all polarize at the same time. You'll be watching and all of a sudden every single window in the place will darken to maximum opacity." Sharma leaned back in the seat, her eyes still on the house. "Sometimes I think there's a whole network of people in there waiting for a signal—as if they all had something important to transmit but had to block surveillance first so no one could monitor. Why else polarize the windows in an autonomous zone? And then as soon as the place is secured they all begin transmitting—and that's why the house moves."

Moss whistled.

"No, I don't need a vacation."

An autonomous vehicle glided silently past the windshield. Sharma started and bumped her knee on the steering column.

"No, you don't need a rest," Moss said. "You're starting to see moving houses, hear phantom transmissions. You've got deviations in your brain, Sharma, algorithms of fatigue, subroutines of irrationality—"

At that moment, all at once, every last window in the house darkened to maximum opacity.

The street was quiet and still, not a movement, not a sound. Moss and Sharma both leaned forward, as if waiting for the ghostly transmissions to commence.

The house began to move.

It shifted from side to side, it rolled forward and back, it swayed and dipped and twisted, straining at the anchor of its foundation. The house could have been preparing to disconnect and roll down the...

Moss looked at Sharma and Sharma looked at Moss and then they both looked back at the moving house.

"And the power," Sharma said. "The power he uses! He could be running the most energy-intensive operation in the district. He could have a whole server farm of computational systems, and he still wouldn't need all that power."

The agent had picked up the profile. He thumbed through the pages now in amazement. "Where do you get a guy like this?" he asked. "Did you see what he's researching?"

"And navigation systems won't work on this street."

The agent lit a cigarette and sighed.

He usually sighed when making the decision to investigate a dwelling. It expressed his weariness and distaste for people who went off and got deviant when they could be enjoying a happy, normal existence. There was something implacable about his sighs.

"He'll be coming out soon," Sharma said. "He has dinner next door with a widow. Then he goes to the archives. Always the same. Dinner at the widow's next door and then the archives."

Moss's eyebrows went up a fraction of an inch. "The archives?" he said. "Is he in with that bunch?"

Sharma nodded.

"Should be very interesting," Moss said slowly.

"I can't wait to see what he's got in there," Sharma murmured, watching the house with a consuming interest.

They sat there in silence and every now and then their eyes widened as the house performed a new movement.

Schultz stopped on the porch to brush the tracking powder off his shoes. He hadn't seen the patrol car and this intense preoccupation of his was also responsible for the moving house—he simply hadn't noticed. There was a certain amount of vibration, of course. He had a bootleg connection into the autonomous vehicle charging grid, and the high-voltage current caused some oscillation against the thin walls of the house. At least, he called it oscillation; he'd never thought to watch from outside.

He went in and threw his jacket on the sofa, there being no room left in the closets. Crossing the living room he stopped to press a button.

Every window darkened to maximum opacity.

"Secure as a vault," he thought, satisfied. He continued on toward the closet at the foot of the stairs and then stopped again. Was that right? No, tight as a encrypted file. He went on, thinking: The old systems.

The downstairs closet was like a great control panel, a profusion of switches surrounding the Master Controller, which was a miniature traffic simulator that processed 365.25 scenarios per hour. The switches had a curious elegance about them. They were all quite old, salvaged from manual vehicles and control towers and they activated in graceful sequences at the rate of 30 and 31 times an hour... although there was one slightly eccentric relay that vacillated between 28 and 29. He watched as they clicked and flashed in the darkness, and then set them for seven o'clock in the evening, April seventh, any year.

Outside, the autonomous zone vanished.

It was replaced by an illusion. Or, as Schultz hoped it might appear, the illusion of the autonomous zone vanished and was replaced by a more satisfactory, and, for his specific purpose, more functional, illusion. Looking through the window he saw only a highway.

Instead of algorithm-controlled vehicles at perpetual optimal flow, there were manually-driven cars moving chaotically, marred only by an occasional collision which left the smell of burning rubber in the air. There was also a gigantic billboard. It dominated a huge area of sky, and it advertised. The cars and billboard both looked down upon a highway that was itself chaotic, composed largely of individual decisions.

Individual choice, he thought, and freedom. Satisfactory. And dinner for two. Blast, he'd never be able to figure that one out! He watched as the billboard displayed, "Drive Your Own Destiny" and the manually-driven cars flashed slowly from red to violet taillights, then went back to the closet and turned on the sound. The house began to fill with the roar of engines as the billboard shifted to "Freedom Means Choice."

He rubbed his chin critically. It seemed all right. A chaotic highway, an advertising billboard, vehicles, sound. They were all purely speculative of course. He had no idea how manual driving really felt—or looked for that matter. Not to mention a billboard. But then, neither did the widow. He'd have to be confident, assertive. Insist on it. I tell you, my dear, this is a genuine realistic manual highway. Now, does it do anything to your sense of autonomy? Do you feel the thrill of individual decision-making?

His own sense of autonomy didn't seem to be affected. But then he hadn't read that book on ancient transportation and trade policy customs.

How really odd the ancients were. Courtship seemed to be an incredibly long and drawn-out process, accompanied by a considerable amount of inefficiency. Communication seemed virtually impossible. "No" meant any number of things, depending on the emotional intelligence of the speaker and the circumstances. It could mean yes, it could mean ask me again later this evening.

He went up the stairs to the bedroom closet and tried the weather-maker, thinking roguishly: Thou shalt not flood. The risks he was taking! A light rain fell on the highway and speakers began to play romantic music. Undiminished, the giant billboard and the chaotic traffic continued to be prominent, although the traffic occasionally collided and demolished several of the lane markers.

The last switch in the bedroom closet was a rather elegant control lever from an old 1995 manual transmission. This was on the bootleg connection; he gingerly moved it.

Far below in the cellar there was a rumble and then the soft hum of power came to him.

He went downstairs to watch out the living room window. This was important; the window had a really fixed attitude about power surges. The lane markers bent and sparked against each other as the power rose and the billboard shook a trifle as it whispered "Choose Your Own Path."

He watched with folded arms, considering how he would start. My dear Mrs. Hamilton. Too formal. They'd be looking out at the chaotic highway; time to be a bit forward. My very dear Mrs. Hamilton. No. Contrived. How about a simple, Dear Susan. That might be it. I was wondering, seeing as how it's so late, if you wouldn't rather stay over instead of going home...

Preoccupied, he hadn't noticed the power building up, didn't hear the shaking and rattling of the connections. There were attic connections linked to wall connections and wall connections linked to cellar connections, and they made one gigantic network that began to overload and surge as high-voltage current from the autonomous vehicle grid rushed in, slowly opening the manual transmission lever wider and wider...

The lane markers thrashed about, short-circuiting each other. The chaotic traffic shot off sparks and then quickly disappeared from sight. The billboard fell on the highway and rolled ponderously along, displaying "Freedom Has Consequences."

The shaking house finally woke him up. He scrambled upstairs to the manual transmission lever and shut it off.

At the window again, he sighed. Repairs were in order. And it wasn't the first time the power got out of control.

Why didn't she marry him and save all this bother? He shut it all down and went out the front door, wondering about the logic of the months, about structured August and eccentric February and romantic April. April. Its days were thirty and it follows September. And all the rest have thirty-one. What a strange people, the ancients!

He still didn't see the silver car parked down the street.

"Men are too fragile," Susan Hamilton said over dinner. "For all practical purposes I'm never going to marry again. All my husbands malfunction."

"Would you pass the asparagus, please?" Arthur Schultz said.

She handed him a platter of steaming green asparagus. "And don't look at me that way," she said. "I'm not going to marry you and if you want reasons I'll give you four of them. Robert. James. William. And Thomas."

The widow was an intense woman. She did everything intensely—talking, cooking, dressing. Her asparagus was intensely green. Her clothes rustled and her jewelry clinked and her voice resonated. She was possessed by an uncontrollable energy. Schultz had never known anyone like her. "You forgot to season the potatoes," she said intensely, then went on as calmly as it was possible for her to be, to explain why she couldn't marry him. "Do you have any idea what people are saying? They're all saying I'm cursed! I drain my husbands of their vitality and when they're depleted I carry their bodies outside on my way to city hall."

"As long as there are people," he said philosophically, "there'll be gossip."

"But it's the environment! Why don't they talk about that? The environment is toxic, I'm positive. It's not nourishing. The environment is toxic and Robert, James, William and Thomas couldn't stand it. Poor Thomas. He was never so healthy as on the day he was born. From then on things got steadily worse for him."

"I don't seem to mind the environment."

She threw up her hands. "You'd be the worst of the lot!" She left the table, rustling and clinking about the room. "I can just hear them. Try some of the salad. Five. That's what they'd say. That woman did it again. And the plain fact is I don't want you on my record."

"Really," Schultz protested. "I feel splendid. Never better."

He could hear her moving about and then felt her hands on his shoulders. "And what about those very elaborate plans you've been making to convince me?"

Schultz froze with three asparagus spears hanging from his fork.

"Don't you think they'll find out? I found out and you can bet they will. It's my fault, I guess. I talk too much. And I don't always tell the truth. To be completely honest with you, Dr. Schultz, it wasn't the old customs at all standing between us, it was environment. I can't have another man malfunction on me, it's bad for my self-esteem. And now you've gone and done something illegal and peculiar."

Schultz put his fork down. "Dear Susan," he started to say.

"And of course when they do find out and they ask you why, Dr. Schultz, you'll tell them. No, no heroics, please! When they ask a man a question he always answers and you will too. You'll tell them I wanted to be courted and when they hear that they'll be around to ask me a few questions. You see, we're both a bit deviant."

"I hadn't thought of that," Schultz said quietly.

"Oh, it doesn't really matter. I'll join Robert, James, William—"

"That won't be necessary," Schultz said with unusual force. "With all due respect to Robert, James, William and Thomas, I might as well state here and now I have other plans for you, Susan."

"But my dear Arthur," she said, leaning across the table. "We're trapped, you and I."

"Not if we could leave the autonomous zone," Schultz said quietly.

"That's impossible! How?"

In no hurry, now that he had the widow's complete attention, Schultz leaned across the table and whispered: "Manual control, Susan? Space? Miles and miles of space where the traffic algorithms have no control whatever? Where the wind blows across highways; or is it the other way around? No matter. How would you like that, Susan?"

Breathing somewhat faster than usual, the widow rested her chin on her two hands. "Pray continue," she said.

"Endless vistas of individual choice and freedom? April roads, Susan. And June, which as you may know follows directly upon April and is supposed to be the month of brides, of marrying. June also lies beyond the autonomous zone."

"I see."

"And," Dr. Schultz added, his voice a honeyed whisper, "they say that somewhere out in the space and the freedom and the individual choice, the sleeping manual transmission awakens and engages because on a certain day it's spring and that's when it roams the Open Highway where algorithms no longer calculate."

"My." Susan Hamilton rose, paced slowly to the window and then came back to the table, standing directly over Schultz. "If you can get us outside the autonomous zone," she said, "out where a man stays vital long enough for his wife to get to know him... if you can do that, Dr. Schultz... you may call me Susan."

When Arthur Schultz stepped out of the widow's house, there was a look of such intense abstraction on his features that Sharma felt a wistful desire to get out of the car and walk along with the man. It would be such a deliciously deviant experience. ("April has thirty days," Schultz mumbled, passing them, "because thirty is the largest number such that all smaller numbers not having a common divisor with it are primes." Moss frowned and added it to the profile. Sharma sighed.)

Pinning his hopes on the Movement, Schultz went straight to the archives several blocks away, a neglected depressing place given over to government records and censored old files with redactions in them. It was used so infrequently that the Movement was able to meet there undisturbed. The archivist was a weathered, obsolete woman of eighty. She spent her days reading ancient transportation logs and, like the files around her, had been rendered by time's own censor into near unintelligibility.

"Here's one," she said to him as he entered. "Manual Vehicle Registration. Issued to Jennifer Alvarez on March 14, 1979 for five years. What do you make of it?"

In the litter of files and records and dried out ink stamps that surrounded the archivist, Schultz noticed a torn poster with a curious illustration. "What's that?" he said.

"A highway," she replied quickly. "Now listen to this. Seven years later on March 21, 1986, Antonio Harper took out the same registration. What do you make of that?"

"I'd say," Arthur Schultz said, "that he... that he recommended it to her, that one day they met on the street and he told her about this registration and then they... they went to the office together and she registered it and eventually, why eventually they got married."

"Hah! They were brother and sister!" the archivist shouted in her parched voice, her old bureaucratic eyes laughing with cunning.

Schultz smiled weakly and looked again at the poster. The highway was unquestionably a transportation phenomenon. It stretched ominously, like a malevolent ribbon, and coursed the countryside chaotically, carrying individuals to destinations. He couldn't help wondering if highways did anything to feminine pulses, if they could possibly be a part of a romantic evening, with dinner and freedom. He absently stuffed the poster in his pocket and went on into the other rooms, the archivist mumbling after him: "Katherine Rodriguez, April 21, 1991," as though reading inscriptions on a tombstone.

The Movement met in what had been the research room, where unpaid scholars of the afternoon had once upon a time studied records for other people's projects. The members sat around at the standard tables looking oddly like giants fled from their algorithms, protesting.

"Where did the old society fail?" the leader was demanding of them. He stood in the center of the room, leaning on a heavy walking stick. He glanced around at the group almost complacently, and waited as Arthur Schultz squeezed into an empty chair. "We live in an autonomous zone," the leader said, "for lack of something. A decision! What is the one thing that the great technological societies before ours could not automate, notwithstanding their various artificial intelligences, electronic and otherwise?"

Schultz was the kind of man who never answered a rhetorical question. He waited, uncomfortable in the standard chair, while the others struggled with this problem in revolutionary logic.

"A sound trade policy," the leader said, aware that no one else had obtained the insight. "If a sound trade policy can't be automated the only alternative is not to have any trade policy at all. Thus the movement into autonomous zones began—by common consent of the governments. This is known as self-regulation."

Logically out in left field, Arthur Schultz waited for a lull in the ensuing discussion and then politely inquired how it might be arranged for him to get out.

"Out?" the leader said, frowning. "Out? Out where?"

"Outside the autonomous zone."

"Oh. All in good time, my friend. One day we shall all disconnect and leave."

"And that day I'll await impatiently," Schultz replied with marvelous tact, "because it will be lonely out there for the two of us. My future wife and I have to leave now."

"Nonsense. Ridiculous! You have to be prepared for the Open Highway. You can't just up and leave, it would be suicide, Schultz. And logically very poor."

"Then you have discussed preparations, the practical necessities of life on the Open Highway. Food, fuel, a map perhaps? What else? Have I left anything out?"

The leader sighed. "The gentleman wants to know if he's left anything out," he said to the group.

Schultz looked around at them, at some dozen pained expressions.

"Tell the man what he's forgotten," the leader said, walking to the far window and turning his back quite pointedly on them.

Everyone spoke at the same moment. "A sound trade policy," they all said, it being almost too obvious for words.

On his way out the archivist shouted at him: "Water Management Records, thirty-five years overdue!" She was calculating the fine as he closed the door.

Arthur Schultz's preoccupation finally came to an end when he was one block away from his house. It was then that he realized something unusual must have occurred. A silver patrol car of the security authorities was parked at his front door. And something else was happening too.

His house was moving.

It was disconcerting, and at the same time fascinating, to watch one's residence oscillating on its foundation. It was such a strange sight that for the moment he didn't give a thought to what might be causing it. But when he stepped gingerly onto the porch, which was doing its own independent vibration, he reached for the doorknob with an immense curiosity.

The door flung itself open and knocked him back off the porch.

From a prone position on his minuscule front lawn, Schultz watched as his favorite reading chair sailed out of the living room on a blast of electromagnetic interference and went spinning down the avenue in the bright sunshine. A wild surge and a thick static poured out of the house. It brought chairs, clothes, small tables, lamps trailing their cords, tablets, sofa cushions. The house was emptying itself fiercely, as if purging an old, corrupted system. From deep inside he could hear the rumble of his ancient server rack as it rolled ponderously from room to room.

He stood up; a charged field swept over him, crackling at his face, standing his hair on end. It was a buzzing in his ears, and a tingle on his skin. He got hit by a shoe.

As he forced his way back to the doorway waves of interference played over his face and he heard a voice cry out from somewhere in the living room.

"Help!" Agent Moss called.

Standing in the doorway with his hair standing on end, the interference crackling about him, the server rack rumbling in the distance like thunder, Arthur Schultz suddenly saw it all very clearly.

"Power," he said in a whisper.

"What's happening?" Moss yelled, crouching behind the sofa.

"Grid power," he said.

"What?!"

"Overload surge!"

The interference crackled for a moment and then Moss's lost voice emerged from the chaos of the living room. "These are not Optimal Traffic Conditions!" the voice wailed. "The speed is not 45 mph. The density is not 23 vehicles per mile!"

Schultz held his face up to let the static wash over it. "Individual choice!" he shouted. "Freedom! My soul for manual control!" He grasped the doorway to keep from being blown out of the house.

"Are you going to make it stop or aren't you!" Moss yelled.

"You'll have to tell me what you did first!"

"I told her not to touch that lever! Sharma. She's in the upstairs bedroom!"

When he heard this Schultz plunged into the house and fought his way up the stairs. He found Sharma standing outside the bedroom with a lever in her hand.

"What have I done?" Sharma asked in the monotone of shock.

Schultz took the lever. It was from a 1995 manual transmission.

"I'm not sure what's going to come of this," he said to Sharma with an astonishing amount of objectivity, "but the entire autonomous vehicle charging grid is now flowing through my bedroom."

The interference screamed.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

"Not any more there isn't."

They started down the stairs carefully, but the surge caught them and they quickly reached the bottom in a charged heap.

Recruiting Agent Moss from behind his sofa, the three carefully edged out of the house and forced the front door shut.

The interference died. The static dispersed. They stood tingling in the Optimal Traffic Conditions of the bright avenue.

"I never figured on this," Sharma said, shaking her head.

With the front door closed the power quickly built up inside the house. They could see the furnishings whirl past the windows. The house did a wild, energized dance.

"What kind of a place is this?" Moss said, his courage beginning to return. He took out his tablet but it was completely fried. He tossed it away.

"Sure, he was different," Sharma murmured. "I knew that much."

When the roof disconnected they weren't really surprised. With a certain amount of equanimity they watched it lift off almost gracefully, standing on end for a moment before toppling to the ground. It was strangely slow motion, as was the black spinning vortex that now rose out of the master bedroom, spewing data and devices every which way.

"Now what?" Moss said, thoroughly exasperated, as this strange black vortex began to accelerate, whirling about like some malevolent algorithm...

Arthur Schultz took out the poster he'd found in the archives. He held it up and carefully compared the spinning vortex in his bedroom with the illustration. The vortex rose and spun, assuming the identical shape of the illustration.

"It's a data storm," he said softly. "A network data storm!"

"What," Moss asked, his bravado slipping away again, "what... is a data storm?"

The data storm roared and moved out of the bedroom, out over the rear of the house toward the edge of the autonomous zone. "It says here," Schultz shouted over the roaring, "that individuals traveled from controlled zones to free territories in data storms and that... and that free territories are wonderful and mysterious lands beyond the confines of algorithmic living."

Moss's eyes and mouth were great zeros.

"Is there something I can turn?" Sharma asked.

Huge chunks of infrastructure began to fail around them.

"Schultz!" Moss shouted. "This is a direct order! Make it go back!"

Schultz stared at the cascading failures spreading across the district. For a long moment, he watched the autonomous vehicles swerving at frightful angles, depleted of charge, rushing to the charging stations which they quickly overwhelmed. The algorithm-controlled traffic vanished behind the mushrooming data storm. Optimal conditions collapsed across entire blocks.

The infrastructure failure was spreading rapidly now—power substations sparked and went dark, navigation beacons flickered out, the carefully maintained grid that kept twenty-three vehicles per mile at precisely forty-five miles per hour was disintegrating before their eyes.

Moss grabbed Schultz's arm. "You have to stop this! The whole district is going down!"

Schultz pulled free and began running toward the next house. "Mrs. Hamilton!" he shouted. "Susan!"

Behind him, Moss stood frozen, watching the destruction spread. His tablet was destroyed. His car was powerless. The entire surveillance network he relied upon was collapsing into chaos. He looked at the data storm with something approaching horror.

Sharma, standing beside him, watched Schultz disappear around the corner of the Hamilton house. "He's actually going to do it," she murmured, and there was something in her voice that might have been admiration.

"Do what?" Moss demanded. "Destroy everything? Look at this mess!" He gestured at the sparking substations, the wandering vehicles, the darkened houses. "Years of infrastructure optimization, gone! The traffic patterns alone will take months to recalibrate!"

"He's going to escape," Sharma said quietly.

Moss turned to stare at her. "Escape? Into that?" He pointed at the data storm, which was now a towering black spiral reaching toward the edge of the autonomous zone. "That's not escape, that's suicide!"

But even as he spoke, they could see two figures emerging from the Hamilton house—Schultz and the widow, hand in hand, running toward the vortex.

"Stop them!" Moss shouted, but his voice was lost in the roar of failing systems.

Sharma didn't move. She watched as the two figures grew smaller, watched as they approached the spinning darkness at the boundary of everything she had spent her career protecting. The data storm seemed to reach down for them, seemed to open like a doorway.

"The whole district," Moss was saying, his voice cracking. "The whole district is going to have to be rebuilt from scratch. Do you understand what this means? The optimization protocols, the traffic algorithms, the surveillance networks—everything! All because that lunatic couldn't leave well enough alone!"

The two figures disappeared into the vortex.

The data storm began to move, carrying them toward the edge of the autonomous zone, toward the Open Highway, toward a place where decisions were still made by humans, where the epistemology of control gave way to the archaeology of freedom, where the linguistics of algorithms dissolved into the simple language of choice.

Sharma and Moss stood in the wreckage of the Valleyview District, watching the storm recede. Behind them, autonomous vehicles wandered aimlessly, their algorithms confused and corrupted. Power flickered on and off across the neighborhood. The silver patrol car sat dead at the curb, its enhanced display dark.

"All of this," Moss said, his voice hollow. "All of this destruction. And for what? Some romantic notion about manual control?"

Sharma said nothing. She was thinking about the pleasantly absurd conversation she'd once had with Schultz, about the fine robust deviant she'd watched for months, about the way his house moved and his windows darkened and his power consumption defied explanation.

"We'll have to file a report," Moss continued, mechanically. "Catastrophic infrastructure failure. Unauthorized grid access. Deliberate sabotage of autonomous systems." He looked around at the chaos surrounding them. "They'll want to know how this happened. They'll want to know who's responsible."

The data storm was a distant smudge now, barely visible against the horizon. Somewhere beyond it lay the Open Highway, and April roads, and June weddings, and a lifetime of manual control.

"He got what he wanted," Sharma said finally.

Moss stared at her. "What?"

"Schultz. He got what he wanted. He escaped."

"And destroyed half the district doing it!" Moss kicked at a piece of debris. "When I get my hands on that lever—" He stopped, remembering. The lever was gone, pulled from its housing by Sharma, now lying somewhere in the rubble of Schultz's bedroom. The bootleg connection was severed. The damage was done.
